# Chachakka Sutta (MN 148 (PTS MN iii 280))

**ID:** MN 148 (PTS MN iii 280)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Chachakka Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Six By Six
**PTS:** MN iii 280
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn148

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Chachakka Sutta* ("Six By Six", MN 148) is the 148th discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, situated in the *Salāyatanavagga* of the *Uparipaṇṇāsa* [Bendall 1893; SuttaCentral]. In this discourse, the Buddha systematically analyzes sensory experience through six groups of six factors—internal bases, external bases, classes of consciousness, contact, feeling, and craving—and demonstrates the emptiness and lack of an ontological self across all of them [SuttaCentral; Roach 2014; Watanabe 1983]. It delineates the cognitive sequence (*phassa* → *vedanā* → *taṇhā*) and explains how feeling conditioned by contact can trigger underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), such as aversion arising from painful feeling [Lin 2015; Webster 2005]. Because of its elegant, highly structured numerical exposition of insight, modern scholars note its proto-Abhidhamma character, noting affinities with the numerical matrices of texts like the *Dharmaskandha* [Sujato 2012; Watanabe 1983]. At its conclusion, sixty bhikkhus are said to have attained arahantship [Sujato 2012; Sujato 2001]. In Sri Lankan tradition preserved in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the celebrated preacher Maliyadeva thera famously recited the sutta across numerous vihāras (including the Lohapāsāda), each time leading sixty monks to arahantship [Adikaram 1946].

Curated parallels include *Saṁyuktāgama* sūtras (SĀ 304, SĀ 323–327, SĀ 330), the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra* (chapter 4), Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SHT sutta 71, SF 18), Śamathadeva's *Upāyikā* (Up 3.059), as well as internal Pali parallels such as SN 35.60, SN 12.44, MN 18, and MN 38 [SuttaCentral; Lin 2015]. Machine alignments computed by DharmaNexus agree extensively with these identifications, registering strong text-reuse matches with the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* (score 75), *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35, 529 matches), *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12), and MN 137 (*Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta*) [DharmaNexus]. Notably, while the Pali version presents the cognitive process successively and records sixty arahants, SĀ 304 presents contact as giving rise to feeling and craving together without mentioning this mass attainment [Lin 2015; Sujato 2012].
